title: Chaos Engineering & Reliability Testing for Data

scenes.heading: Chaos Engineering
scenes.subheading: Break it on purpose to build confidence
scenes.narration: Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures into your systems so you discover weaknesses on your own terms, not during a real outage.

scenes.heading: Why break things on purpose
bullets: Failures are inevitable — better to rehearse them
Untested failover paths often don't actually work
Builds real confidence in recovery procedures
scenes.narration: Failures are inevitable, so it is far better to rehearse them under controlled conditions than to discover them at three in the morning. Failover paths that were never tested surprisingly often fail to work when you finally need them. Injecting chaos reveals hidden dependencies and false assumptions, and each successful experiment builds genuine confidence in your recovery procedures.

scenes.heading: The chaos experiment method
scenes.narration: A chaos experiment begins by defining the steady state, the normal metrics that mean the system is healthy. You form a hypothesis that the system will tolerate a specific failure. Then you inject that failure in a controlled way, measure whether steady state held, and fix whatever weakness the experiment exposed.

scenes.heading: Data-specific chaos
scenes.narration: Traditional chaos targets infrastructure by killing nodes, adding latency, or failing over regions. Data chaos is unique to pipelines and tests how they cope with late-arriving records, injected schema drift, or duplicated events. Exercising both kinds ensures your pipeline is resilient not just to broken machines but to broken data.

scenes.text: Start small with a tight blast radius and a kill switch, ideally in staging. The goal is learning, not causing a real incident.
scenes.narration: Start small with a tightly controlled blast radius and a ready kill switch, ideally in staging first, because the goal of chaos engineering is learning, not triggering a genuine incident.
